meta.titre: Transformers: turns ratio, efficiency and power transmission

sections.contenu_markdown: Charging a phone in Kumba, running a radio in Bafia or lighting a school in Ngaoundere all begin with mains electricity at 240 V or more, which is far too high for most small devices. The little black box between the socket and your phone charger contains a transformer, and the large metal boxes on electricity poles in every town contain bigger ones. The GCE regularly asks for the output voltage of a transformer, the current in one of its coils, and the reason why electricity is sent over long distances at very high voltage.

items: An electric current in a coil produces a magnetic field around it.
A changing magnetic field passing through a coil induces a voltage in it.
Electrical power is the product of voltage and current, $P=VI$, and is measured in watts.

sections.titre: How a transformer works: turns ratio, power and efficiency
sections.contenu_markdown:
A **transformer** changes the size of an **alternating** voltage. It has a **primary coil** (input) and a **secondary coil** (output) wound on the same **laminated soft-iron core**.

**How it works.** The alternating current in the primary coil produces a changing magnetic field in the iron core. This changing field passes through the secondary coil and induces an alternating voltage in it. Direct current gives a steady field, which does not change, so no voltage is induced: **a transformer does not work with d.c.**

**Transformer equation** (turns ratio):

$$\frac{V_s}{V_p}=\frac{N_s}{N_p}$$

where $V$ is the voltage and $N$ the number of turns on the secondary (s) and primary (p) coils.

- **Step-up transformer:** $N_s>N_p$, so $V_s>V_p$.
- **Step-down transformer:** $N_s<N_p$, so $V_s<V_p$.

**Ideal transformer (100 % efficient):** power in = power out, so

$$V_pI_p=V_sI_s$$

A step-up transformer gives more voltage but **less current**; it never gives more power.

**Efficiency of a real transformer:**

$$\text{efficiency}=\frac{P_{out}}{P_{in}}\times100\,\%=\frac{V_sI_s}{V_pI_p}\times100\,\%$$

**Energy losses** in a real transformer: heat in the copper coils (resistance of the wire; thick copper wire reduces it); **eddy currents** in the core (a laminated core, made of thin insulated sheets, reduces them); the core is repeatedly magnetised and demagnetised (a soft-iron core minimises this) and some magnetic field leaks out of the core.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked why power stations use step-up and step-down transformers.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Power lost as heat in the cables is $P_{loss}=I^2R$. For a given power $P=VI$ delivered, raising the voltage lowers the current in proportion, and because the loss depends on $I^2$, a tenfold higher voltage means a hundred times less energy wasted. So a step-up transformer at the power station raises the voltage (to many thousands of volts) for transmission, and step-down transformers near towns lower it to $240\ \mathrm{V}$ for homes.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a transformer is used to run a battery-type device such as a radio or a phone charger.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Many devices need a low voltage d.c. supply. A step-down transformer first lowers the a.c. mains voltage, then a **rectifier** (diodes) changes it into d.c. This is why a mains adaptor contains a transformer and a diode circuit.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A step-down transformer used to run a lamp has $2000$ turns on the primary coil and $100$ turns on the secondary coil. The primary is connected to the $240\ \mathrm{V}$ a.c. mains. A lamp of resistance $3\ \Omega$ is connected to the secondary coil.

(a) Calculate the output voltage.

(b) Calculate the current in the lamp and the output power.

(c) The transformer is ideal. Calculate the current in the primary coil.

(d) In practice the primary current is $0.25\ \mathrm{A}$. Calculate the efficiency.

etapes.action: Use the turns ratio to find $V_s$.
etapes.justification: The ratio of voltages equals the ratio of turns.

etapes.action: Find the current in the lamp.
etapes.justification: Apply Ohm's law to the lamp: $I=V/R$.
Power is voltage multiplied by current.

etapes.action: Find the primary current for an ideal transformer.

etapes.justification: Compare the useful output power with the input power $V_pI_p$.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **(a)** $12\ \mathrm{V}$. **(b)** $4\ \mathrm{A}$ and $48\ \mathrm{W}$. **(c)** $0.20\ \mathrm{A}$. **(d)** Efficiency $=80\,\%$; the other $12\ \mathrm{W}$ is wasted as heat in the coils and core.

items.pourquoi_faux: The turns ratio is inverted. More turns on the secondary give a larger secondary voltage.

items.erreur_markdown: “A transformer works from a car battery because a battery supplies electricity.”
items.pourquoi_faux: A battery gives direct current. The magnetic field in the core is then steady and induces no voltage in the secondary coil.
items.correction_markdown: A transformer needs an alternating (changing) current in its primary coil.

items.erreur_markdown: “A step-up transformer gives more power than it receives.”
items.pourquoi_faux: Energy cannot be created. The output voltage is larger, but the current is smaller, and the power out is at best equal to the power in.
items.correction_markdown: For an ideal transformer $V_pI_p=V_sI_s$; for a real one $P_{out}<P_{in}$.

items.erreur_markdown: “The core is made of one solid block of iron to carry the magnetic field better.”
items.pourquoi_faux: A solid block lets large eddy currents flow in it, which heat the core and waste energy.
items.correction_markdown: The core is built from thin sheets of soft iron, insulated from each other (laminated), to reduce eddy currents.

items.pourquoi_faux: This is upside down and would give more than $100\,\%$ for a real transformer.

items.enonce_markdown:
A transformer has $500$ turns on the primary coil and $50$ turns on the secondary coil. The primary voltage is $220\ \mathrm{V}$.

(a) Calculate the secondary voltage.

(b) Is it a step-up or a step-down transformer?

A school demonstration uses an ideal step-up transformer which changes $12\ \mathrm{V}$ a.c. into $240\ \mathrm{V}$ a.c. The primary coil has $100$ turns and the output power is $60\ \mathrm{W}$.

(a) How many turns are on the secondary coil?

(b) Calculate the current in the secondary coil and in the primary coil.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\dfrac{N_s}{N_p}=\dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{240}{12}=20$, so $N_s=20\times100=$ **$2000$ turns**.

(b) Secondary: $I_s=\dfrac{P}{V_s}=\dfrac{60}{240}=$ **$0.25\ \mathrm{A}$**.

Ideal transformer: $P_{in}=P_{out}=60\ \mathrm{W}$, so $I_p=\dfrac{60}{12}=$ **$5\ \mathrm{A}$**. (The step-up transformer has a smaller secondary current.)

items.enonce_markdown:
A power station sends $100\ \mathrm{kW}$ along cables of total resistance $5\ \Omega$.

(a) Calculate the current in the cables and the power wasted as heat if the power is transmitted at $10\,000\ \mathrm{V}$.

(b) Repeat the calculation if it is transmitted at only $1000\ \mathrm{V}$.

(c) Use your answers to explain why a step-up transformer is used at the power station.

(d) Explain why a battery cannot replace the alternating supply.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $I=\dfrac{P}{V}=\dfrac{100\,000}{10\,000}=$ **$10\ \mathrm{A}$**. Power wasted $=I^2R=10^2\times5=$ **$500\ \mathrm{W}$**, which is only $0.5\,\%$ of the power sent.

(b) $I=\dfrac{100\,000}{1000}=$ **$100\ \mathrm{A}$**. Power wasted $=100^2\times5=$ **$50\,000\ \mathrm{W}$**, which is $50\,\%$ of the power sent.

(c) Ten times lower voltage means ten times more current, and the heat loss $I^2R$ becomes a hundred times larger. A step-up transformer raises the voltage so the current is small and little energy is wasted in the cables.

(d) A battery gives d.c. and a transformer only works with a changing current; a d.c. supply produces no changing field in the core and no secondary voltage.

items_markdown: A transformer changes an alternating voltage using two coils on a laminated soft-iron core; it does not work with d.c.
Turns ratio: $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p}=\dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$. Step-up: more turns on the secondary. Step-down: fewer turns on the secondary.
Ideal transformer: $V_pI_p=V_sI_s$. Efficiency $=\dfrac{V_sI_s}{V_pI_p}\times100\,\%$ and is always below $100\,\%$ in practice.
Losses: heat in the coils, eddy currents in the core, repeated magnetisation of the core and leakage of magnetic field.
Electricity is transmitted at high voltage because a smaller current wastes less energy ($P_{loss}=I^2R$).
